tldr: Instead of generating articulated 3D assets one by one, an LLM agent creates category-level procedural generators. This framework cuts model call costs to about $0.05 per asset while automatically producing over 400,000 high-quality articulated objects.
hero_caption: A comparison of paradigms for constructing articulated 3D assets. While manual annotation and per-asset agentic synthesis are costly, the proposed RFW-A has agents build reusable category-level generators, enabling low-cost sampling of vast, diverse assets purely through procedural execution.
overview:
For robots to manipulate doors, drawers, and household appliances in the real world, simulation environments need massive quantities of "articulated 3D assets" with accurately defined joint axes, part hierarchies, and physical properties. However, manual modeling and articulation annotation take over ten minutes per asset, demanding enormous human effort. While recent approaches use LLM agents to write code automatically, they repeat expensive reasoning and debugging for every single asset, resulting in soaring API costs and runtimes.

The authors observed that objects in the same category share construction logic and part connectivity rules, even when their appearances and dimensions vary. This led to a key insight: rather than having agents synthesize assets directly, why not have them write category-level procedural generators capable of producing diverse variations? Once a generator is completed and passes verification, endless variations can be produced simply by changing the random seed, incurring zero extra model calls or token costs.

This work formalizes this idea as "RFW-A" and builds "RFW-A-400K," a massive dataset containing over 400,000 assets across more than 500 categories. Beyond rigorously testing physics simulation stability and kinematic correctness, the authors show that training on this dataset significantly boosts part-level articulation estimation from single-view meshes. Furthermore, manipulation policies trained in simulation transfer zero-shot to real-world robots.
contributions: Proposed RFW-A, a framework where LLM agents construct and validate reusable category-level procedural programs, enabling large-scale sampling without repeated model inference.
Constructed and released RFW-A-400K, a collection of 402,410 sim-ready articulated assets across 500+ categories with rigorous articulation definitions, PBR materials, and physical properties.
Reduced generator authoring costs to an average of $0.05 per asset when amortized over 200 samples, cutting API expenses by roughly 23x compared to per-asset agentic synthesis baselines.

Demonstrated that training with the generated assets enhances generalization in articulation estimation, and that program parameter editing enables an 80% zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer success rate in real robot manipulation.

sections.heading: Moving from Per-Asset Generation to Agent-Authored Category Generators
sections.summary: Articulated assets are vital for robot learning, yet manual creation is labor-intensive and per-asset LLM synthesis is prohibitively expensive. This paper tackles the bottleneck at its root by having agents construct shared, category-level procedural generators.
sections.details:
For objects with movable parts like furniture, appliances, and tools, kinematics—how parts are connected and move—is just as crucial as visual geometry. However, manually annotating parent-child part hierarchies, joint ranges, friction, and mass is tedious, taking over ten minutes per asset even with specialized tools.

Procedural generation (rule-based modeling via code) is an attractive alternative, but hand-crafting rules for every category places a huge burden on human designers. Conversely, recent LLM agent-based code synthesis automates the process, yet repeating inference and trial-and-error from scratch for every asset causes token costs to surge.

The authors noticed that cabinets, for example, share the same underlying logic—such as placing top/side panels and drawer rail layouts—across variations. Shifting the role of agents from "per-asset synthesis" to "category generator authoring" allows the initial code authoring cost to be amortized over countless subsequent samples.

RFW-A-400K, built using this framework, contains over 400,000 assets—about 37 times larger than Articraft, the largest prior articulated dataset. While authoring a generator incurs an average API cost of $10.62, sampling 200 assets drops the per-asset cost to just $0.05, making it more than 23 times cheaper than the $1.24 per-asset synthesis baseline.

captions.F2: Variations of cabinets produced from a shared generator. In addition to changes in width and color, variations such as increasing drawer tiers, sliding doors, and flap doors are procedurally generated while preserving shared assembly logic.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Articulated Assets: From Manual Work and Reconstruction to Agentic Synthesis
sections.summary: Movable asset research has evolved from static 3D repositories to scan reconstruction, diffusion models, and per-asset program synthesis. RFW-A bridges the gap between the scalability limits of manual rules and the redundant inference costs of agentic synthesis.
sections.details:
### Articulated Object Datasets
Existing datasets like PartNet-Mobility have supported robotics research with rigorous articulation annotations, but their reliance on manual curation capped category breadth and diversity. While recent efforts incorporate physical properties and real scans, they do not retain the underlying generative programs, making it difficult to freely re-sample shapes and structures.

### Articulated Object Reconstruction and Generative Models
Reconstructing articulated models from sensor images, videos, or 3D Gaussian Splatting is an active area of study. However, these methods focus on digital twins that faithfully replicate specific real objects; they are ill-suited for hallucinating occluded regions or synthesizing novel shapes. Generative models like diffusion frameworks also struggle to guarantee collision-free kinematic motion and exact part connectivity.

### Procedural Generation and Agentic Synthesis
Procedural approaches such as Infinigen-Articulated achieve robust code-based shape generation, but rely on human engineers to design the generation programs. Conversely, recent LLM systems that write articulation code (such as LAM and Articraft) successfully automate authoring, yet synthesize and debug code on a per-asset basis, leading to high inefficiency. RFW-A combines the strengths of both: agents construct procedural generators, which then scale up purely through code execution.

sections.heading: A Four-Agent Collaborative Pipeline for Generator Authoring
sections.summary: RFW-A autonomously constructs robust generators through the coordination of four agents: the Source Agent extracts parts from existing code, the Architect Agent designs blueprints, the Code Agent writes executable programs, and the Repair Agent verifies and fixes failures.
sections.details:
The RFW-A architecture takes a category instruction $c$ and a pool of existing CAD/3D code $\mathcal{A}$ to construct a reusable generator $S_c$.

### 3.1 Agentic Generator Construction
Construction proceeds through the collaboration of four agents:
- **Source Agent**: Searches existing assets for component code matching the category instruction. For instance, when building a "Mars rover," it retrieves wheel code from mobile robots and arm code from robotic manipulators.
- **Architect Agent**: Organizes the retrieved components into a category blueprint graph $\Sigma_c$. Nodes represent component roles, variable parameters, and optional conditions; edges define joint connection rules and parametric relationships.
- **Code Agent**: Implements the executable Python generator code $S_c$ based on this blueprint.

### 3.2 Procedural Execution and Variation Sampling
Providing the completed generator with a random seed $z$ compiles the asset without any additional LLM inference. It first samples free parameters $\chi_z$, resolves dependent parameters and joint states $q_z$ according to blueprint rules, and calls component synthesis routines to output visual meshes and URDF files.

### 3.3 Verification, Auto-Repair, and Release
A program that outputs one valid shape might still fail under different parameter configurations. The Revision Module enforces strict testing:
- **Consistency Checks**: Verifies ahead of time that all branches and variables in the blueprint are reachable in code.
- **Geometric and Motion Tests**: Checks for self-penetration and collisions across rest states, full joint motion ranges, and coupled kinematic states.
- **Repair Agent Fixes**: When failures $\mathcal{F}_t$ such as penetration are detected, the Repair Agent modifies the blueprint or generator code based on diagnostic feedback. This loop iterates until all test cases pass, releasing only thoroughly validated generators.

captions.F4: The generator authoring and execution pipeline of RFW-A. (a) Agents extract components from existing code to construct blueprints, (b) generate executable code followed by testing and automatic repair, and (c) sample diverse variations from validated generators simply by changing the seed.

sections.heading: 400K Sim-Ready Assets: Physical Property Grounding and Direct Parameter Editing
sections.summary: The constructed generators sampled over 400,000 simulation-ready assets across 500+ categories. Every asset includes PBR textures and grounded physical parameters, while supporting intuitive 3D modification via parameter editing.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Dataset Overview and Scale
The resulting RFW-A-400K dataset contains 402,410 articulated assets across more than 500 categories. It provides visual meshes, collision meshes, part kinematic hierarchies, articulated joint parameters in URDF format, and the exact seeds and parameter configurations needed for reproducibility.

Quality is maintained throughout: all 400K released assets achieve a 100% kinematic pass rate, meaning zero degenerate joint definitions. Furthermore, amortizing authoring costs across generator runs enabled scaling at an estimated API cost of just ~$0.05 per asset.

### 4.2 Material Grounding and Direct Editing
To reproduce physical dynamics faithfully in simulation, surface materials and physical properties are essential. RFW-A builds a curated library of 8,295 high-grade PBR (Physically Based Rendering) materials spanning 124 material classes.
Each material is linked to six physical parameters in SI units: density, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, static and dynamic friction coefficients, and restitution. During asset generation, materials are sampled from this library based on surface IDs emitted by the generator, assigning consistent visuals and physical attributes.

Moreover, programmatic generation enables direct 3D editing. Instead of manipulating mesh vertices manually, users can simply modify exposed parameters—such as swapping component types, altering grid counts, resizing dimensions, or changing materials—and rerun the code, producing desired alterations without breaking kinematic validity.

captions.F7: The automatic material and physical property grounding process. Based on surface class IDs emitted by the generator, appearance (PBR textures) and six physical properties (density, friction, elasticity, etc.) are jointly assigned to the asset from the material pool.
captions.F8: Examples of direct 3D editing enabled by procedural programming. (a) Modifying leg geometry, (b) changing fence slat counts, (c) swapping chair materials, and (d) resizing cabinet dimensions are all executed instantly without kinematic failure.

sections.heading: Part-Level Articulation Estimation from Single Meshes: Strong Out-of-Domain Generalization
sections.summary: On predicting part segmentation and joint kinematics from a single 3D mesh, models trained on RFW-A-400K significantly outperformed prior datasets (PartNet-Mobility and Articraft), demonstrating marked accuracy gains even on unseen categories.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Using the "Particulate-B" model, which estimates movable parts and joint parameters from a single 3D mesh, the authors evaluated performance gains across training datasets. Three setups were compared under identical training steps (150K) and batch sizes (128): (1) PartNet-Mobility (PM) alone, (2) PM combined with Articraft, and (3) PM combined with RFW-A-400K.

### Metrics and Results
Evaluations were conducted on two splits: an "In-Domain" split (255 categories seen in training) and a "Category-OOD" split (774 unseen categories excluded from all training sets). Metrics included resting and max-articulation part-level IoU (mIoU, gIoU), part Chamfer distance (PC), and overall Chamfer distance (OC).

The results demonstrated clear advantages:
- **In-Domain Performance**: PM + RFW-A-400K achieved top scores across all metrics. Compared to PM + Articraft, resting mIoU improved by 7.43 points, max-articulation gIoU by 10.13 points, and movable part Chamfer distance (PC) dropped significantly from 0.10196 to 0.06268.
- **Category-OOD Performance**: RFW-A-400K also led across all five part-level metrics on unseen categories. Notably, max-articulation gIoU improved by 19.2% and resting PC improved by 19.0% over Articraft.

Qualitative comparisons showed that while models trained on prior datasets missed drawers or misaligned joint axes, models trained on RFW-A-400K faithfully captured intricate structures, confirming that massive, structurally sound data directly yields superior generalization.

captions.F9: Comparison of articulation and part estimation from single meshes. From top to bottom: PM alone, PM + Articraft, proposed (PM + RFW-A-400K), and Ground Truth (GT). As highlighted by red circles and arrows, the proposed method accurately recovers fine structural supports and movable part geometry.

sections.heading: Aligning to Reality via Program Editing: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
sections.summary: Policies trained in simulation using RFW-A assets were deployed on real robots without any real-world fine-tuning. Fine-tuning generator parameters to match physical setups boosted task success rates from 62% to 80%.
sections.details:
### Real-World Manipulation Tasks
To test how well RFW-A-400K assets serve as simulation proxies for real-world robot learning, the authors evaluated five tasks with distinct kinematics:
1. Opening and closing a round cabinet door (bimanual coordination)
2. Unfolding a folding ruler straight
3. Folding a folding chair
4. Depressing a toaster lever
5. Closing double doors

### Training and Evaluation Protocol
For each task, the closest matching asset was retrieved from RFW-A-400K. Three simulation training regimes were compared:
- **Retrieval**: Uses only the single retrieved asset in simulation.
- **Retrieval + 4 Edit**: Adds 4 parameter-edited variations adjusting dimensions and layout toward the physical object.
- **Retrieval + 9 Edit**: Adds 9 edited variations in the same manner.

All settings maintained identical demonstration counts (500 demos), policy architectures, and training steps. The trained policies were evaluated on a physical dual-arm robot setup over 10 trials per task.

### Real-Robot Results
Real-robot success rates improved monotonically from 6.2/10 (62%) with Retrieval alone, to 7.2/10 (72%) with 4 edits, and reached 8.0/10 (80%) with 9 edits. Tasks sensitive to dimensions and resistance, such as pushing the toaster lever or opening the cabinet door, saw the largest improvements. Expanding simulation diversity toward real-world configurations via parameter editing—without collecting extra demonstrations—served as a crucial bridge for closing the Sim-to-Real gap.

captions.F10: Zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer across five articulated object manipulation tasks. The top row shows simulation training scenes, and the bottom row displays the corresponding real-robot evaluation setups.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: A Scalable Foundation for Embodied AI
sections.summary: By unifying procedural generation and agentic reasoning, RFW-A achieves large-scale, low-cost synthesis of collision-free articulated assets, establishing a solid foundation for both robotic perception and control.
sections.details:
This work resolves the tension between the high inference costs of agent synthesis and the heavy manual effort of procedural modeling by shifting to category-level generator synthesis. The resulting RFW-A-400K is not merely a collection of 3D shapes, but a highly practical dataset equipped with precise kinematics, PBR materials, and grounded physical quantities directly applicable to physics simulation.

Future opportunities include scaling this foundation to train vision-language-action (VLA) models involving bimanual and whole-body coordination, as well as extending the approach to interactive 4D modeling of complete scenes.

sections.heading: Appendix: Rigorous Simulator Compatibility Tests and Data Quality Validation
sections.summary: Using a Core-200 subset across four major physics engines—Genesis, PyBullet, MuJoCo, and Isaac Sim—the authors demonstrated exceptional simulation numerical stability with a 99.5% pass rate.
sections.details:
### Simulator Compatibility and Numerical Stability
Even syntactically valid URDF files frequently crash physics engines due to inconsistent mass matrices or exploding collision contacts. Using a representative "Core-200" subset from each dataset, the authors ran 1-second passive rollouts with the root link fixed across four leading physics engines: Genesis, PyBullet, MuJoCo, and Isaac Sim. RFW-A-400K achieved a 99.5% pass rate across all four simulators, confirming stability free from numerical explosions.

### Quantifying Structural Diversity
To measure kinematic tree diversity, the authors computed normalized Tree Edit Distance (nTED). RFW-A-400K achieved the highest score at 0.453. In addition, 84.65% of its assets feature multiple joints, demonstrating that rather than mass-producing simple single-axis hinges, the dataset comprehensively covers complex, multi-joint topologies.

sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations: Challenges of the Current Approach
sections.summary: Key remaining challenges include the generator diversity's reliance on initial component pools, incomplete search over continuous parameter spaces for collisions, and physical values grounded under reference conditions.
sections.details:
While RFW-A is highly capable, several limitations remain:
- **Dependence on Initial Components**: The structural variety a generator can synthesize is constrained by the expressive range of the code and blueprints the Source Agent starts with. Creating entirely new mechanical mechanisms requires continuous expansion of the source code pool.
- **Finite Testing Coverage**: Although the Revision Module evaluates sampled configurations and motion states, it cannot mathematically guarantee zero collision across the entire continuous parameter space.
- **Accuracy of Physical Grounding**: Material properties like friction and elasticity are reference table estimates under standard conditions, rather than precision measurements capturing real-world wear or individual manufacturing differences.

takeaways: Having LLMs write category-level procedural generators instead of single assets dramatically cuts generation costs down to ~$0.05 per asset.
Integrating kinematic motion tests and collision checks into an automated revision loop allows agents to build robust articulated assets that do not break physics simulators.
Pre-training on high-quality, diverse articulated data substantially improves out-of-domain generalization in part-level articulation estimation.
Procedural programs allow straightforward parameter editing, and feeding real-aligned parameter variations into training significantly boosts zero-shot Sim-to-Real success rates.
limitations: Mechanism diversity is constrained by the initial library of source programs and component building blocks.
Self-collision checking during motion is evaluated on sampled joint configurations, leaving continuous state spaces not exhaustively verified.
Physical attributes tied to PBR materials (such as friction and Young's modulus) are nominal reference values, not individualized real-world measurements.
